statuses.text:
fun fact: i used ai to replace a few tools in my saas businesses

I consider myself experienced and it took me weeks to make sure they work reliably. 

It saved me around $400-500/mo which a good amount for a solo business and makes a difference in my life. Yet it was not the right way to spend my time. 

The two reasons I did it, it was:

1. I love building so it was hella fun.
2. X doomers got in my head and I was trying to save money for the upcoming SaaSapocalypse

In retrospect, i think it was a waste of time and i should have focused my this time on my products. 

Also, it's kinda embarrassing but all these might have been a way to avoid spending time on marketing. 

Building with AI feels so productive yet it's a huge trap when you build, build, and build without any marketing actions.

quote.text:
Love these takes because they make you think...

From one side, he's 100% right. I've replace most of the overpriced saas tools i used with in-house app. 

AI is capable of building anything now. Most saas will struggle and be dead soon, if they dont adapt. Especially the overpriced apps that used to be monopolies and charged crazy amounts for nothing  (eg email sending apps). 

On the other side, in real life, not a single persons cares about vibe coding. 

I can't see my gym coach vibe coding his own client management system, and to be honest, I don't want to see this. As a coach he has to focus 100% on his craft and use AI to adapt his workout programming, not use AI to build apps. 

For me, software is dead only if you sell to indie hackers, and people who have the agency or will to build on their own apps. 

Professional who really values their time, they won't waste time on vibe coding. They'll pay a monthly fee to outsource it on a saas and they'll focus on their craft.

It doesn't really matter if it's a progressive tax system or not.
 
When you reach the 45% threshold you have basically zero incentive to work more because you lose half of your money.

Paying 45% in tax is insane. 

A similar tax structure exist for sole proprietorship companies in my country Greece too. 

On my second freelancing year, I hit the threshold and I immediately stopped taking new project. It didn't worth the effort.

Hopefully, you can switch to a different company structure and pay a fixed 22% tax, so i did this next year.

quote.text:
Germany does NOT take 50% tax of everything you make.

Germany has a progressive income tax system. Meaning:
- You don't pay the highest rate on your full income.
- You only pay it on the part above the threshold.
- The max income tax rate is 45%.
- Everything below that is taxed in lower brackets.

So no, if someone in Germany makes $117k, the government doesn't just take half.

For companies, it's different. Corporate tax, trade tax, distributions, etc.

Germany has many problems for founders. But let's at least hate on the correct ones.

No one seems to grasp that you'll have to spend years of sleepless nights to make it and margins will be much lower.

Another EU masterpiece to silently kill its small businesses. 

They make it practically impossible to sell physical products across EU countries

quote.text:
The EU's new packaging regulations will profit Amazon & Temu and make it nearly impossible for smaller European players to sell across the Union.

Why? It requires a representative in EVERY EU country to sell across the Union, ending the single market.

Instead of one set of rules and one registration that works across the Union, we get 27 national compliance regimes stacked on top of each other. The cost and administrative burden are manageable for Amazon and Temu. They already operate at continental scale and can absorb the paperwork. For a small manufacturer or online seller in Portugal, Poland or Sweden who wants to reach customers in other EU countries, it will simply be impossible. The representative fees, reporting, and legal risk end the margin before the first order ships.

The result is predictable: European small and medium companies retreat to their home market while the foreign platforms can grow in their own market and then expand across the EU with their scale. We are told this is about the environment and the circular economy. In practice it is regulatory protectionism for the largest players, dressed up as green policy.

A real single market would mean one registration, one set of standards, and free movement for goods sold by Europeans to Europeans. What we get is more fragmentation, more bureaucracy, and another structural advantage handed to non-European players. This is how you slowly hollow out the European economy.

Hundreds of small businesses have indicated they will stop selling across the EU by August 12th, when the regulation gets into effect. Retreating to their home country only.

The EU must stand for simplification, and harmonisation across Europe. Not regulations which only the big international players can be compliant with. Why are we doing this to ourselves?
